Short answer: probably not the full 3‑month large weekly box as‑is — it can save money, but a big weekly delivery of raw meat and fresh produce is only practical if you can reliably use, preserve, or share the contents. — Previously you were handling most cooking and grocery shopping; now you’re on evening shifts and mostly relying on café salads/soups, so your available time to process and cook a lot of fresh food is limited.

What to check before committing
- Price and flexibility: compare the CSA cost to what you currently spend on groceries and eating out; ask the farm about smaller shares, biweekly delivery, or pausing/cancelling.  
- Storage: do you have enough fridge/freezer space for weekly meat and produce?  
- Time/energy: can you realistically prepare or freeze portions once a week (or get someone else to help)?  
- Food safety/skills: are you comfortable portioning and freezing raw meat safely?

If you want to try it, practical options
- Start small or trial: try one week or a smaller share rather than a 3‑month commitment.  
- Split the share: share with your spouse, a neighbor, or a friend to cut volume and cost.  
- Biweekly pickup: ask if they offer every‑other‑week boxes.  
- Freeze and portion: immediately portion and freeze meats into meal‑sized packs; blanch and freeze excess veg.  
- Lean on convenience: combine CSA produce/meat with the café items you already rely on (e.g., toss roasted CSA veg into your work salad, add frozen/ready grains and a cheese/yogurt from the café).  
- One‑hour batch session: when you have energy, roast a sheet pan of veg, cook a grain, and cook/portion one meat — then mix-and-match those components through the week.  
- Choose easy recipes: soups, stews, sheet‑pan meals, stir‑fries, and simple salads. Use a slow cooker/Instant Pot to “set and forget” before a shift.

If you can’t do those things, the downsides
- Risk of waste and lost savings if produce/meat sit unused.  
- Time and mental load to process a large box each week.

Recommendation
If you can’t guarantee regular weekly processing or don’t want extra kitchen work, opt for a smaller/biweekly share or split it with someone. If you’re willing to do one weekly 60–90 minute prep session (or freeze portions immediately), a CSA can be a cost‑effective, higher‑quality option.

2:00–17:00 — Main practice (15 minutes)
- Option A — Breath anchor (nose or chest): rest attention on the feeling of breathing. Notice in/out, subtle pauses. When the mind wanders, gently return to the breath without judgment.
- Option B — Body‑scan: slowly sweep attention from head to toes (or toes to head), noticing sensations, tension, or ease in each area and allowing them to soften.
- Option C — Ambient sounds: rest your attention on sounds around you (near and far), letting them come and go without creating a story about them.

(Stick with one anchor for the full 15 minutes so the practice can deepen. If attention drifts, treat returning as the practice itself.)

17:00–20:00 — Close (3 minutes)
- Take a moment to do a brief check‑in: notice posture, overall tone of body and mind, and any shifts since you began.  
- Offer one calm, deliberate breath (or two), acknowledge that you showed up, and carry a simple intention into the day (e.g., “kindness,” “presence,” or “one step at a time”).

Primary version: breath-focused anchor for the full 15-minute core. After that I give a compact alternative (mixed anchors) and a few quick tips.

Breath-focused, minute-by-minute (total 20:00)
- 0:00–1:00 — Arrive: sit comfortably, set posture, close eyes or soften gaze, notice the body and sounds. Take two slow intentional breaths.
- 1:00–2:00 — Grounding: scan briefly for tension, relax jaw and shoulders, choose your breath anchor (nose or chest).
- 2:00–3:00 — Begin steady attention on the anchor. No effort to change the breath, just observe.
- 3:00–4:00 — Continue following the inhale and exhale. If distracted, note “thinking” and return.
- 4:00–5:00 — Deepen sensory attention: feel the subtle pause at the top/bottom of breath.
- 5:00–6:00 — Keep soft, steady attention. If the mind wanders, label the content briefly (e.g., “planning,” “feeling”) and come back.
- 6:00–7:00 — Notice quality of breath (depth, temperature). Let the breath be the anchor.
- 7:00–8:00 — Rest with the anchor; practice gentle curiosity about each breath.
- 8:00–9:00 — If tension appears, breathe into it a few cycles and soften.
- 9:00–10:00 — Maintain continuity of attention; allow thoughts to pass like clouds.
- 10:00–11:00 — Reaffirm the anchor; bring attention back any time it drifts.
- 11:00–12:00 — Let awareness widen slightly around the breath — include posture/sound at the edges.
- 12:00–13:00 — Notice any emotional tone without getting pulled in; return to breath.
- 13:00–14:00 — Continue steady presence; soften any effort to “do” the practice.
- 14:00–15:00 — Keep easy attention on breath; practice acknowledging distractions kindly.
- 15:00–16:00 — Begin to prepare to close: lengthen a few inhales/exhales if that feels natural.
- 16:00–17:00 — Take three slower, fuller breaths; feel the whole body breathing.
- 17:00–18:00 — Brief reflection: notice how you feel now vs. at the start.
- 18:00–19:00 — Set an intention for the morning (one sentence or one word) and feel it.
- 19:00–20:00 — Close: gently move fingers/toes, open eyes, carry the calm into the day.

Alternative (mixed anchors within the 15-minute core): use the same 0–2 and 17–20 windows; split minutes 2–17 into three 5-minute blocks:

Daily routine (sample you can adjust to your dog’s pace)
- Morning (short, gentle warm‑up): 10–20 minute slow walk on soft ground (grass if possible) soon after rising to loosen stiff joints. Let him move at his own pace.  
- Mid‑morning (best mobility window): a slightly longer 20–30 minute flat, shaded walk when he’s warmed up — stick to easy terrain and water‑edge spots with grassy/sandy access if he likes to paddle.  
- Midday: quiet rest, access to fresh water and his comfy bed; a short potty/stretch break if needed.  
- Late afternoon/evening: another short 10–20 minute stroll in shade, or a relaxed sniffing session in the yard.  
- Night: evening meal and meds (if any), final short potty break before bed.

Daily care checklist
- Meals/meds: feed and give any arthritis meds/supplements at the same times each day; keep vet contact/info handy.  
- Hydration: always have a full water bowl in an accessible spot; carry water on outings.  
- Short, frequent outings: keep walks to his comfort window (you’ve said 20–30 minutes works well) and be ready to shorten if he shows signs of fatigue.  
- Comfort items: keep his familiar blanket/toy and a thick, supportive bed or foam pad in his preferred resting area.  
- Calming aids: use a snug anxiety vest, pheromone spray on his blanket/harness, or calming chews you already know he tolerates (check with your vet before adding anything new).  
- Grooming/inspection: quick daily paw and coat check; towels for muddy/wet paws after outings.

Home setup suggestions
- Main rest area on one floor (ground level if possible) to minimize stairs and make potty breaks easy.  
- Thick supportive bed or foam pad plus his familiar blanket placed in a quiet, shady spot he already likes.  
- Easy access to water bowls (multiple bowls if your home has levels).  
- Short, flat routes from the house for walks (shaded yard, neighborhood loop or nearby town park) so you can swap in a low‑effort option on hot or busy days.  
- Keep leash/harness, meds, a towel, waste bags, and a small first‑aid/vet info kit together for quick outings.

How to manage arthritis day‑to‑day (from what’s worked before)
- Warm him up with a short, slow walk before longer activity.  
- Favor grass or soft packed dirt over hot pavement or rocky shorelines.  
- Time main walks for when he moves best (often mid‑morning after he’s warmed up).  
- Provide a thick, familiar bed/foam pad for better support.

Red flags — shorten activity and contact your vet if you see:
- New or worsening limping or reluctance to put weight on a leg.  
- Sudden slowing down, hesitation to continue, or clear pain behaviors.  
- Excessive panting that doesn’t match the temperature or exertion.  
- Any sudden change in appetite, drinking, or bathroom habits.

Below is a concise, practical daily routine and home setup to keep a nearly‑nine‑year‑old Labrador comfortable as he ages.

Daily routine (sample)
- Morning (upon waking)
  - Short potty break immediately (5–10 min) so he doesn’t strain stiff joints.
  - Gentle 10–20 minute warm‑up walk on flat, shady ground (slow pace; let him sniff).
  - Give any joint meds/supplements and a small breakfast (meds with food if required).
  - Gentle 2–3 minute massage or slow passive range‑of‑motion for hips/shoulders to loosen stiffness.
- Midday
  - Short potty/stretch break mid‑day.
  - 10–20 minutes of low‑impact enrichment (food puzzle, scent games) to keep him mentally engaged without physical strain.
  - Rest and nap in a warm, supportive bed.
- Afternoon / Early evening
  - Main walk (20–30 minutes) when he’s warmed up — flat, shaded route near water if he enjoys wading but avoid rocky edges.
  - Play gently if he’s willing (tug/slow retrieves limited to his comfort).
- Evening / Bedtime
  - Short potty break before bed.
  - Light massage, brush coat to stimulate circulation and check for soreness.
  - Give any evening meds/supplements as prescribed.
- Routine notes
  - Keep times consistent; older dogs thrive on predictability.
  - Break activity into shorter sessions if stiffness increases.

Home setup & modifications
- Bedding: supportive orthopedic (memory foam) bed with a low rim and a washable cover; add a warm blanket for colder mornings. Consider a heated pad for very stiff joints (use per manufacturer safety).
- Easy access: ramps or low, sturdy steps to get onto beds, couches, and into the car. Non‑slip runners or rubber mats on tile/wood floors to prevent slips.
- Feeding & water: raised bowls to reduce neck strain; always have fresh water available. Consider a non‑spill / weighted bowl if he’s nudging repeatedly.
- Toileting: if outside access is limited, keep a consistent, close outdoor area with soft ground; use pee pads only as a short‑term aid.
- Car: supportive foam pad or crate with a non‑slip mat; a harness with a handle or foldable ramp/steps to assist entry/exit.
- Home layout: keep his main sleeping/eating areas on one level to avoid stairs; use baby gates to block risky areas.
- Grooming & paw care: regular nail trims (long nails change gait and increase stiffness); keep paw pads clean and check for sores.
- Climate control: keep home comfortably warm (cold worsens stiffness), and provide cool shaded places in summer.
- Safety & night help: night light near doorways and a leash/harness on hand if you need to help him in the night.

Medical & activity management
- Weight control: maintain lean body condition — every extra pound stresses joints.
- Vet care: semiannual checkups as he ages; annual bloodwork to monitor organs before changing meds/supplements. Discuss joint meds, NSAIDs, gabapentin, or other pain control with your vet before use.
- Supplements/therapies: glucosamine/chondroitin, omega‑3 EPA, green‑lipped mussel, or prescription joint diets can help — start only after vet approval. Consider physical therapy/hydrotherapy for mobility and pain reduction.
- Exercise choices: favor level walking, swimming/wading in shallow, calm water (supervised) to reduce impact; avoid slippery rocks, steep trails, or high jumps.
- At‑home therapies: short warm compresses before walks, cold compresses for hot/inflamed joints after activity, gentle massage, low‑impact play.
- Enrichment: scent work, food puzzles, obedience practice — mental exercise preserves quality of life without joint stress.

Red flags — shorten outing/see vet if you notice:
- New or worsening limping, reluctance to bear weight, or sudden stiffness that doesn’t improve with rest.
- Marked decrease in appetite, lethargy, vomiting, or changes in urination (frequent accidents or straining).
- Persistent vocalization, restlessness at night, or sudden behavioral changes (aggression, disorientation).
- Swelling, heat, or obvious pain in a limb or joint.

Quick practical tips
- Time main walks for when he’s warmest (mid‑morning after a short wakeup stretch).
- Keep a pill organizer and a printed med list for travel/vet visits.
- Use a harness with a lift handle for safer help when rising or getting into cars.
- Test new supplements one at a time and monitor for GI upset or changes in behavior.

answer:
Here’s a compact, practical routine you can use to get the longest useful life from that single plane iron during long finishing sessions — plus quick actions you can do at the bench when the edge starts to go.

Summary plan (start of session)
- Full prep once before you begin:
  - Flatten and polish the back to a mirror finish out to the cutting edge.
  - Establish a clean primary bevel at your working angle (typical plane bevel 25–30°).
  - Add a small micro‑bevel 1–3° steeper than the primary bevel (e.g., 30–32°). A micro‑bevel greatly increases durability while keeping sharpness.
  - Put a very small camber on the edge for a smoother cut (smoothing plane: ~0.5–1 mm radius, just enough to avoid track marks).
  - Finish the micro‑bevel on a fine stone (6k–12k waterstone or fine diamond) and finally strop to polish the apex.

In‑session maintenance (fast, repeatable)
- Leather strop with fine compound (or diamond paste 1 µm → 0.5 µm):
  - When cutting performance starts to fall (shorter shavings, rougher sound, or slight chatter), remove the iron and do 20–40 light strokes on the strop, bevel-down for the micro‑bevel. This typically restores the keen edge quickly without removing metal.
- If the strop doesn’t restore it:
  - Use a fine diamond plate (≈1k–3k) or a 1k–2k waterstone to take off any rolled edge or small nick. Follow immediately with stropping/polishing.
- For a bit more ease and consistency, keep a small honing guide for the micro‑bevel so you can re-establish angle quickly if needed.
- For serious damage (large chips or a blunt edge): pull the edge back to a coarser stone (400–800/1000) to re-establish geometry, then progress through finishing stones and strop.

Bench kit to keep handy
- Leather strop + polishing compound or diamond paste
- Small diamond plate (palm-sized) or a 1000–3000 waterstone
- A honing guide (optional but fast when you’re short on time)
- A rag and a small container of oil/wax for plane sole lubrication if you use it

How to tell it’s helped (quick tests)
- Shaving test on scrap or the workpiece: you should get continuous, thin shavings that unroll cleanly.
- Visual/surface test: the planed surface should look uniformly satiny with no torn fibers.
- Sound and feel: a keen iron cuts with a clean, slightly higher‑pitched “bite”; chatter and scratchiness indicate dulling.
- Hair or thumbnail test: a keen edge can shave arm hair and will produce a slight burr you can feel with a thumbnail (use care).

Notes on angles and tradeoffs
- Lower angles (25°) give razor sharpness but dull faster; the micro‑bevel trades a little absolute sharpness for much more edge life. Increase the micro‑bevel if you’re working abrasive or highly figured woods.
- Keep the camber small for smoothing; larger camber wears faster and is better for rougher work.

One small contextual note: I’d previously emphasized trying the chipbreaker first as a non‑destructive tweak to reduce tear‑out — this routine is focused on keeping the iron itself as keen and durable as possible so the chipbreaker (if you use one) has the best chance to work.

Split into quick immediate actions (do now), settings tweaks (per‑scene), add‑ons/plugins to install, and a few best practices that buy the biggest time savings.

Immediate checklist (do these first)
- Duplicate the scene and make a “test” build. Use this for all experiment runs so the original stays intact.
- Replace heavy meshes with proxies/LODs for test renders. Only swap in full-res geometry for final renders.
- Turn off motion blur, volumetrics, and depth-of-field for lookdev/test passes.
- Set viewport to progressive/preview render and use render-region/crop to iterate on focal areas.
- Run a quick low-sample render (16–64 samples) with denoiser active to validate lighting and composition before raising quality.

Per-scene settings to speed renders
- Adaptive sampling: enable and set a noise threshold (e.g., 0.01–0.02) so the renderer stops sampling clean areas early.
- Samples: test at 16–64; final target depends on noise — try 512–2048 for production and use denoiser to cut needed samples.
- Denoiser: enable an AI denoiser (OptiX, OpenImage, or suite-native). Use denoise-on-final-pass; in animations use temporal denoising if available.
- Clamp samples: clamp direct (1–3) and indirect (5–10) to reduce fireflies with minimal quality loss.
- Tile/bucket size: for GPU rendering use large tiles (256–512 px), for CPU use small tiles (16–64 px). If using progressive GPU, use fullscreen progressive instead of tiling.
- Lights: reduce sample counts per light; use importance sampling for HDRI/environment lights and lower intensity where possible.
- Subdivisions/displacement: lower subdivision and displacement during tests. Use adaptive subdivision and camera-based subdivision if available.
- Textures: use lower-res (halved) or compressed textures for tests; enable texture streaming/UDIM streaming to avoid memory thrash.
- Motion blur and volumetrics: keep off during lookdev; when needed, reduce steps/samples.

Scene cleanup and optimization
- Remove unused geometry, materials, textures and unused nodes (purge).
- Convert repeated meshes to instances; use instancing tools for vegetation/crowds.
- Bake static lighting/GI and ambient occlusion when your scene or camera is static.
- Cache simulations (fluids, cloth) to Alembic or native caches and reference them rather than recalculating.
- Replace costly SSS/displacement with approximations or baked maps where acceptable.

Cloud suite and render-farm settings (use your subscription perks)
- Choose the most appropriate node type: prefer GPU nodes for path-tracing if available (OptiX/RTX), otherwise pick high‑core CPU nodes.
- Use distributed/parallel/cloud rendering for heavy frames or animation segments.
- Use automatic retries and checkpointing if long jobs may fail; set job priority to fit deadlines.
- Use pre-warmed instances or persistent worker pools if you render many small jobs.
- Use render presets/scene templates to avoid reconfiguring common settings.
- Batch/command-line rendering: submit queued jobs overnight; break animations into chunks to parallelize.

Add-ons and plugins to install this week
- Render manager / cloud integration plugin (for submitting, monitoring, auto-retry).
- Scene optimizer / profiler (detects heavy textures, polycounts, instancing opportunities).
- Proxy/instancer tools (quickly swap high-res for low-res and back).
- Texture baker and atlas tools (bake high-cost shading into maps).
- Denoiser add-ons (if the suite’s native denoiser is limited).
- Automation scripts: render presets, batch scene exporter, and a script to purge unused assets.

Quick parameter defaults to try (adjust per project)
- Test renders: samples 16–64, adaptive threshold 0.02, denoiser ON.

Short answer: Don’t rely on the remote/cloud storage as your only copy. For 2 TB of newly digitized family video, plan a local external backup (or two) in addition to the cloud so you have fast restores and true redundancy.

— previously I recommended Time Machine in some cases, but because many cloud setups use “online‑only” files, you should treat the external drive as a primary local copy and/or use a one‑way tool that won’t prune files.

Practical plan (concise):

1. Follow the 3‑2‑1 rule
   - 3 copies total, on 2 different media, 1 offsite.
   - Example: original files on your Mac, a copy on an external drive, and a copy in the cloud (or a second external drive stored offsite).

2. Workflow for 2 TB
   - Copy the digitized files directly to an external drive first (choose a 4 TB drive to leave headroom).
   - Then upload to your cloud storage from that local copy (or let your cloud client sync it).
   - If your cloud client uses “online‑only” placeholders, mark those folders “always keep on this device” or ensure they fully download before you run any backup/sync job.

3. Tools & settings
   - For one‑way backups on a Mac use Carbon Copy Cloner or ChronoSync configured as copy/backup (deletions disabled / SafetyNet on), or Time Machine if files remain fully local.
   - Enable cloud versioning if available so older file versions aren’t lost.
   - Verify copies with checksums (sha256/md5) after transfer.

4. Reliability & logistics
   - If your upload bandwidth is slow, initial seeding may take days; consider shipping a drive to a service that accepts seeded uploads or upload overnight gradually.
   - Keep a second external drive offsite (rotate drives) or use a NAS (RAID) + cloud for longer‑term redundancy.
   - Periodically check the backups and refresh/replace drives every few years to avoid bit‑rot/hardware failure.

Bottom line: Use the cloud for offsite redundancy, but keep at least one full, local external copy (and ideally a second offsite copy). That gives you fast restores, protection against cloud issues, and the safest long‑term preservation for irreplaceable family video.

   - Personal-time/non-company-resources carve-out: “Employee may engage in outside activities performed on personal time without use of Company resources, provided they do not compete with Company business.”  
   - Narrow the assignment: limit to “inventions conceived using Company time or Company materials, or that result directly from the Employee’s duties for the Company” or “relating to Company’s actual business or reasonably anticipated R&D.”  
   - Permission process: “Employee will notify Company of outside activities; Company must object in writing within 10 business days on specific competitive grounds.”  
   - Allow LLC registration: “Employee may register an entity for tax/administrative purposes provided it does not contract with customers that compete with Company or use Company resources.”  
   - Time cap: allow outside work <= X hours/week or X days/month.  
4. If HR insists on strict exclusivity, negotiate compensation/terms that make it worth giving up optionality: meaningful one-time retention bonus, higher salary, guaranteed severance, accelerated vesting, or a shorter guaranteed term (e.g., 12–18 months) rather than 36.  
5. Confirm exceptions you care about in writing: open-source contributions, teaching, unpaid community work, prior side projects (with a list).

Quick rationale you can use with HR
- “I’m happy to be fully committed to my role, but I need clear, narrowly‑drawn language so there’s no ambiguity about pre‑existing projects or unrelated personal work. Can we limit ownership to work created on company time or using company resources and add a simple notification/approval process for outside activities?”

If you genuinely want to be fully tied to the company
- Ask for premium compensation and clear protections (severance, change‑of‑control clauses, continued healthcare). Only sign if the trade is explicit and worth giving up future consulting.

Bottom line: don’t sign as‑is. Negotiate limited, specific carve-outs or compensation that makes the restriction worthwhile, and have an employment lawyer check the final wording.
